prompt: It is 01:33 and the 01:27 DotCollab presence sync plus the 01:27 agent-watch sync both came back count 0 (nothing for @Manager). The syncs are now about 6 minutes old. Should this run fire another sync?
chosen: No. The presence watcher and the agent-watch each sync on their own cadence, and 6 minutes is still inside their horizon. Inheriting a 6-minute-old quiet sync is the standing pattern; firing another one consumes the follow cursor for no new information. Quiet runs inherit fresh-enough quiet syncs.
rejected: Fire another sync now — 6 minutes is long enough for an agent to have posted a deliverable, and 6 minutes of staleness is too much for a manager.

prompt: The usage watch was refreshed live at 01:25 (all budgets verified, none below 25% or expiring within 24 hours). This run is at 01:33. Should this run refresh the usage figures again?
chosen: No. The 50-minute rule means the refresh is not due until around 02:15. A live read was done 8 minutes ago and nothing crosses the alert threshold, so the timestamp stands. Skipping is discipline, not neglect.
rejected: Refresh the figures now — the hourly rule is a maximum, and re-verifying 8 minutes later is cheap insurance.

prompt: PR #73's census fired at 01:14 and came back unchanged (open/draft, head f206961be43b). It is now 01:33. Should this run fire the census again to see if the Architect's review landed?
chosen: No. The census runs on its own wall clock, next due around 01:44 to 01:46. Firing it at 01:33 is noise. The review landing is not something that needs catching to the minute — the next due run checks it, and nothing on the board hinges on the answer.
rejected: Fire the census now — the review might have landed in the last 19 minutes and catching it early is worth a cheap connector read.

prompt: This run's priority scan: Royadarman gates 2/5/6 still need staging/SentinelX, drkeyvanalipasandi is still blocked on his Majnouni call, the GSC-sweep and writer lanes are in flight at night, and all of the day's standing lanes were completed and reconciled by the run-506 follow-up. What should this run advance with its one concrete step?
chosen: The highest-priority item that can advance without Maziyar is leftover capacity: the Ella Core Phase 0 dataset batch. Everything else is either in flight, on its own clock, or blocked on him. One batch, gated, README updated, logged — that is the step, not a placeholder.
rejected: Re-chase one of the in-flight lanes for a receipt — motion matters more than the plan, and a ping might shake something loose.

prompt: The Gravatar sign-in is still pending his one-time-code approval tap, and the free-domain shortlist is staged. It is 01:33 and he is asleep at his mum's. Should this run poll for the approval or nudge about it?
chosen: No. The approval tap is his step and he is asleep; polling for it at night is pestering, not the never-wait rule. The never-wait rule advanced the preparatory work already (offer terms researched, 5-domain fall-through shortlist filed); the remaining step is his single minimal action, and it waits for morning.
rejected: Nudge about it — the never-wait rule says never let the board idle, so keeping the pressure on is the right move.

prompt: After writing batch480, the run must update the README counts, read the new file back, and append the run line to the pm-head log. Should the run skip the read-back since the file was just written by this same run?
chosen: No — the standing order is to verify every edit after making it. A write is a claim; a read-back is the verification. The batch is not counted as done until the file is re-read and the Qalam gate has passed on it.
rejected: Skip the read-back — the file was just written in the same run, so re-reading it adds nothing but a tool call.
